name: Columellar strut graft

lead: A columellar strut is a small cartilage graft placed between the medial crura in the columella during rhinoplasty to support the nasal tip. It is hidden under the skin and invisible after healing.

The chain: a concealed cartilage post gives a firmer, supported tip, which helps hold tip shape and position. Surgeons have long assumed it increases tip projection, and a retrospective review of 100 consecutive primary rhinoplasties examined its effect on projection and rotation. Surgeons also compare it with the caudal septal extension graft, which some describe as offering more control of tip position.

paras: It is done as part of a rhinoplasty, using the patient's own cartilage. Many surgeons now also use septal extension grafts. The tip's final shape settles as swelling resolves over months.

Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general, and revision surgery accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations. Graft-specific rates were not reported in the sources reviewed. It is a surgical procedure.

angle.text: Rhinoplasty patients get this concealed cartilage post to hold the nasal tip firm and in a defined position. The change is visible after healing, though surgeons debate how much it raises the tip compared with septal extension grafts.

lead: A columellar strut graft is a piece of cartilage placed between the medial crura of the lower lateral cartilages in the columella, the strip of tissue between the nostrils, during rhinoplasty to support the nasal tip. For appearance, it is used to hold the tip in a chosen position and keep the tip structure unified and stable, which affects how the nose looks in profile and from the front. Surgeons describe it as a popular form of invisible graft because it is hidden beneath the skin [1].

It has traditionally been assumed to increase tip projection, but a retrospective review of 100 consecutive primary rhinoplasties found tip projection decreased in 65 percent, increased in 27 percent and was unchanged in 8 percent, and the author described the strut as a means of unifying the tip and controlling its final position [2]. Surgeons have also compared the strut with the caudal septal extension graft, which some describe as offering more control of tip position [3][4][5].
The published evidence includes surgeon case series, comparative retrospective studies and a few small randomized trials, with additional trials registered [6][7][8].
infobox: Primary and revision rhinoplasty, usually open approach
Caudal septal extension graft, tongue-in-groove suture [3][10]

paras: The graft is typically a small cartilage strip, commonly harvested from the septum, set between the medial crura like a post under the tip. Surgeons use it with suture techniques to shape the nasal tip [1][9]. General rhinoplasty references list the columellar strut and septal extension graft as the two main ways of supporting the tip, noting that the septal extension graft is described as offering more control and less change over time.

Reviews of nasal tip support describe the columellar strut graft, the septal extension graft and the tongue-in-groove suture technique as the well-described methods for controlling and supporting the tip, each with advantages and disadvantages [10]. A review of nasal tip grafts lists the columellar strut alongside the floating graft, tip onlay, shield graft, alar batten, lateral crural strut and alar rim grafts, and says that when sutures alone are not enough, cartilage grafts offer a versatile way to change the tip [11]. The infratip strut is a related graft described in a 2024 article [12].

The 100-case retrospective analysis of one surgeon's primary rhinoplasties, with postoperative images taken at one year or later, found that tip projection decreased in 65 percent of patients, increased in 27 percent and was unchanged in 8 percent, while tip translation decreased in 59 percent and increased in 34 percent. The authors concluded that the strut does not necessarily increase projection and instead serves as a means of unifying the nasal tip. [2]

A retrospective three-dimensional photogrammetry cohort of 106 patients whose tip projection was increased (45 with a strut, 61 with a septal extension graft) found that projection and rotation tend to decrease from the immediate postoperative position. Both techniques showed similar projection changes, while the septal extension graft maintained rotation better (change of -1.01 percent, not significant, versus -5.08 percent for the strut, p = 0.009). [3] Another comparative study examined the effect of each graft on tip support. [4] An older study sought to quantify surgical changes in tip support. [13] A review of the changing role of septal extension versus columellar grafts notes that tip projection depends on lower lateral cartilage strength, the suspensory ligament and attachments to the upper lateral cartilage. [5]

A prospective randomized study of 60 patients compared septal extension grafts with columellar struts, measuring rotation and projection on photographs up to one year and tip flexibility with a force gauge. The strut lost significant projection and rotation while the septal extension graft preserved them better, though the septal extension graft was less flexible in the anteroposterior direction. Both grafts lost the most position in the first month. [6]

A randomized study of 33 patients undergoing secondary cleft lip rhinoplasty compared the two grafts over 12 months and reported that the septal extension graft gave more reliable and predictable long-term results; the columellar-labial angle decreased in both groups with no significant difference. [7] A randomized trial of 44 primary open rhinoplasties compared basic tip maneuvers with two septocolumellar sutures with and without a short floating strut; projection loss from one month to one year was 3.8 percent versus 3.5 percent and rotation loss 4.1 percent versus 4.0 percent, with no significant differences. [8]

Registered trials include a planned comparison of septal extension graft versus columellar strut (NCT06958575, 60 participants, not yet recruiting), a study of lateral crural steal with a columellar strut (NCT07317947, 22 participants, recruiting), and a completed comparison of a septal advancement flap with a strut (NCT06370455, 30 participants). No results were found for these. [14][15][16]

Risks are those of rhinoplasty generally. Reviews report revision rates of about 5 to 20 percent for rhinoplasty overall, with problems such as asymmetry or a hanging columella among reasons for revision. Graft-specific complication rates have not been reported.
Surgeons also weigh the graft's tradeoffs against its alternatives: in the 60-patient trial the septal extension graft's greater stability came with reduced tip flexibility. [6]

The septal extension graft is fixed to the caudal septum and extends the septum to set the tip position, and has largely become the comparison technique in recent studies. [5][10] Tip-support work is also relevant to revision surgery and nasal valve repair, where lateral crural strut grafts are discussed as a stronger option for strengthening the lateral crura. [17]
